The reproductive biology of Longface emperor Lethrinus olivaceus has been studied in the waters surrounding the Great Barrier Reef, where a sustained water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] prevails during the summer spawning season. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 12% [GSI = 12%] at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This value, typical for iteroparous lethrinids, suggests a moderate investment in gamete production relative to somatic mass. The onset of reproductive capability is marked by the attainment of a total length of 50 cm [Lp = 50 cm], and at this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 1791 grams [Wwp = approximately 1791 grams]. These size thresholds were derived from extensive sampling of fish caught during commercial and research trawls, with histological examination of gonadal tissue confirming maturity stage.

Newly hatched Lethrinus olivaceus larvae emerge from pelagic eggs that are roughly 0.7 mm in diameter, yielding a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] based on the volumetric relationship for a sphere of that diameter. This minuscule initial mass, comparable to estimates for congeneric species such as Lethrinus lentjan, places the newly emerged yolk-sac larva firmly within the size range typical of small-bodied tropical reef fish larvae. During this lecithotrophic phase, the larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition is a critical bottleneck; survival during this period depends heavily on encountering appropriate zooplankton prey at sufficient densities. Field studies indicate that larval mortality rates are highest during these first few days, a pattern common among pelagic spawners with small egg sizes.

As Lethrinus olivaceus progresses through its life history, it exhibits a substantial increase in body size, culminating in an ultimate total length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters] and an ultimate structural length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] for the largest individuals recorded. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this asymptotic length is estimated at 14127 grams [Wwi = 14127 grams], derived from length-weight regressions calibrated specifically for this species. This maximum size places the Longface emperor among the larger members of its genus, a status likely linked to its predatory role on the reef slope where it preys upon cephalopods, crustaceans, and small fishes. Growth rates are most rapid during the juvenile phase, gradually decelerating as the fish approaches its asymptotic length. Comparative data from otolith microincrement analysis suggest that individuals in warmer, more productive waters may attain a larger ultimate size than conspecifics from cooler or less productive habitats, although the species-level maximum appears to be a robust characteristic of the taxon.

Maximum lifespan in Lethrinus olivaceus has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith age reading, yielding a longevity of approximately 9125 days [am = approximately 9125 days] when maintained at an average ambient temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This remarkable lifespan is among the longest recorded for tropical lethrinids and reflects a slow pace of life characterized by delayed senescence. The species appears to exhibit negligible reproductive senescence even at advanced ages, with gravid females caught at over 20 years of age still producing viable, hydrated oocytes. This pattern stands in contrast to many smaller-bodied reef fishes that exhibit rapid turnover and early mortality. The warm, stable temperatures of tropical coral reef environments may contribute to this extended longevity by reducing the metabolic costs associated with temperature fluctuations, though the precise physiological mechanisms linking temperature to lifespan remain under investigation.

Fecundity in spawning aggregations of the Longface emperor has been quantified by gravimetric counts of hydrated oocytes from gravid ovaries. Females produce a single clutch per spawning event [F_R_i = single clutch per spawning event], and each clutch contains approximately 1,200,000 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch contains approximately 1,200,000 eggs], reflecting the high fecundity typical of broadcast spawners that provide no parental care. This reproductive output, combined with a spawning frequency of several events per season, ensures a continuous supply of pelagic larvae into the plankton. The gonadosomatic index was 12% [GSI = 12%] at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. Further work is required to determine whether spawning frequency varies with female size or age, as has been documented in other large-bodied lethrinid species.
